column35: Blockchain-Based Onsite Activity Management for Smart Construction Process Quality Traceability
column40: Onsite construction activities (OCAs) are essential components affecting construction process quality. Tracing OCAs can control the construction process with high-resolution visibility, help stakeholders demonstrate their compliance with regulations, and reduce interorganizational quality disputes. Traditional technologies cannot meet the information recording demands for traceability, namely, immutability, transparency, and auditability. This work introduces a novel framework for the traceability of OCAs based on computer vision and blockchain technologies. First, cutting-edge deep learning algorithms are introduced to automatically extract OCA information from far-field surveillance videos. Second, a consortium blockchain system is built to record the identified OCA information and the hash value of the raw data for future review. Finally, a case of a high-rise office construction project is used to test and verify the feasibility of the framework, in which a blockchain prototype is developed based on a Blockchain as a Service (BaaS) platform, termly, PolyChain. The experimental results show that the BaaS-based prototype is an effective system architecture with good throughput and latency and can ensure the authenticity and transparency of OCA information for traceability demands. © 2014 IEEE.

column5: The paper addresses the absence of an ethical framework and allocation of corporate digital responsibility (CDR) for the application of digitization and AI in the construction engineering industry. It investigates where CDR can be allocated and how an adequate ethical framework should be designed to support digital innovation while fulfilling EU requirements for trustworthy, human-friendly AI. The study fills a scholarly niche, since no prior study has conceptualized CDR in construction relative to digitization and AI across large, medium, and small companies.

column30: CDR with ethical principles is identified as the key driver for success, efficiency, and sustainability in applying digitization and AI in construction engineering. The study finds that self-commitment is insufficient and that binding legal standards, interdisciplinary academic training, explainable AI, and diversity are needed; innovative companies with value-based cultures outperform conservative ones. Case studies (PERI, Wayss & Freytag, APLEONA) demonstrate that data ownership, data protection, education, and human-centered design are practical barriers requiring ethical and regulatory clarification.
column31: Future research should further develop interdisciplinary ethical frameworks for AI in construction, adapt engineering academic curricula to include technical ethics, and conduct follow-up longitudinal surveys to monitor human-technology relationships. The author calls for expanded investigation into CDR implementation in SMEs, binding European ethical standards for AI, and cross-sector learning to strengthen trustworthy AI 'Made in Germany'.
column32: No prior study has conceptualized CDR in construction engineering in relation to digitization and AI, and related literature (unlike in medicine, automotive, or philosophy) is missing in construction. Ethical principles, diversity considerations, and standards for human-led AI in the construction industry are underdeveloped.

column35: Corporate digital responsibility (CDR) in construction engineering—ethical guidelines for the application of digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) in user practice
column40: Digitization is developing fast and has become a powerful tool for digital planning, construction and operations, for instance digital twins. Now is the right time for constructive approaches and to apply ethics-by-design in order to develop and implement a safe and efficient artificial intelligence (AI) application. So far, no study has addressed the key research question: Where can corporate digital responsibility (CDR) be allocated, and how shall an adequate ethical framework be designed to support digital innovations in order to make full use of the potentials of digitization and AI? Therefore, the research on how best practices meet their corporate responsibility in the digital transformation process and the requirements of the EU for trustworthy AI and its human-friendly use is essential. Its transformation bears a high potential for companies, is critical for success and thus, requires responsible handling. This study generates data by conducting case studies and interviewing experts as part of the qualitative method to win profound insights into applied practice. It provides an assessment of demands stated in the Sustainable Development Goals by the United Nations (SDGs), White Papers on AI by international institutions, European Commission and German Government requesting the consideration and protection of values and fundamental rights, the careful demarcation between machine (artificial) and human intelligence and the careful use of such technologies. The study discusses digitization and the impacts of AI in construction engineering from an ethical perspective. This research critically evaluates opportunities and risks concerning CDR in construction industry. To the author’s knowledge, no study has set out to investigate how CDR in construction could be conceptualized, especially in relation to digitization and AI, to mitigate digital transformation both in large, medium- and small-sized companies. This study applies a holistic, interdisciplinary, inclusive approach to provide guidelines for orientation and examine benefits as well as risks of AI. Furthermore, the goal is to define ethical principles which are key for success, resource-cost-time efficiency and sustainability using digital technologies and AI in construction engineering to enhance digital transformation. This study concludes that innovative corporate organizations starting new business models are more likely to succeed than those dominated by a more conservative, traditional attitude. © 2021, The Author(s).

column5: The construction sector is expected to adopt AI technologies rapidly, but there is limited applied knowledge about the physical and socio-political risks this brings. Existing AI standards, certifications, and safety bodies are insufficient to address sector-specific risks, and regulatory frameworks need to be designed proactively. The paper asks what physical and socio-political risks emerge from 'AI-fication' in construction and how these map to specific activities and stakeholders.

Six overlapping risk categories emerge (unemployment, occupational segregation, accidents, privacy/exploitation, digital risks, decision errors), with liability puzzles intensified by algorithmic opacity. column31: Future work should design country-specific policy frameworks that account for risk perception differences and stakeholder risk tolerance, examining how identified risks interact with national regulatory environments. column35: Towards a responsible integration of artificial intelligence technology in the construction sector
column40: The uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) innovations in the construction industry implies new physical and socio-political risks. Risk analysis is crucial to managing these risks, but is challenging due to the inherent complexity and lack of applied knowledge specific to construction activities. We forecast potential AI innovation trends related to construction from a keyword concurrence analysis of 974 journal articles. We use this analysis to identify potential sector-specific risks in construction activities by forming a risk map based on an analysis of ninety-four articles related to the ethics and impacts of AI technologies. We found that trends in innovation more often involve areas in construction considered 'back-end' tasks, as opposed to 'on-site'. Thus, the potential risks and regulatory challenges from the use of AI technology in the construction sector will be legal, financial, and social, as opposed to risks involving physical harm to users on construction sites. © The Author(s) 2021.

column5: The paper addresses how to ethically and legally implement electronic performance monitoring (EPM), AI-based decision making, and smart contracts for craft workforce management in a Construction 4.0 context. It investigates the legal, ethical, and cultural barriers, particularly GDPR compliance, that arise when collecting, processing, and sharing workers' performance data via wearable sensors, BIM integration, and blockchain. The core problem is balancing technological advancement with worker rights, consent, and trust to prevent human/regulatory factors from becoming bottlenecks to digital transformation.

column30: The paper concludes that implementing Construction 4.0 workforce monitoring requires ethically managed human-machine environments based on pre-established collective agreements, worker awareness, and informed consent. GDPR can act as a bottleneck to digital transformation if human/ethical aspects are improperly addressed, but can also serve as a policy tool for controlling methodologies. Trust (both system-based and cognition-based) between employers and employees is identified as a key enabler, requiring transparent objectives and clear consent protocols.
column31: The authors plan to validate the framework with expert feedback from diverse stakeholders and conduct real EPM field tests to gather insights from craftworkers. These inputs would help refine ethical compliant implementation strategies balancing people, processes, and technology.
column32: The paper identifies gaps in judge-made law interpreting GDPR for workplace monitoring, ambiguity in defining 'biometric data' and 'legitimate interest' for performance monitoring, and the lack of worker-centered ethical frameworks for AI-driven construction management.

column40: Craft workforce is the main productive factor in traditional construction. Construction 4.0 visions are based on automation and digitalisation, meaning that human site activities will require/stipulate changes. The extent to which manual tasks done by humans in construction will be replaced is uncertain. This might vary considering the context or type of work. Construction 4.0 includes craft workforce activities, as these can benefit from technology, fostering digital transformation in the short/medium term. The research scope is workforce-innovation-management using data from job sites. A framework is developed based on data future use involving electronic performance monitoring, building information modelling, smart contracts and artificial intelligence. A systematic scoping review is developed to identify legal/ethical issues in connection to technological aspects. The discussion and findings focus on General Data Protection Regulation compliance to apply the proposed framework. Optimised human-machine-controlled environments must be ethically managed by pre-established collective agreements and must rely on each worker's awareness and consent. The findings suggest that the human aspects if improperly addressed could result in a bottleneck of digital transformation advances. Along with the framework, the paper provides a step-by-step, streamlined review of the regulations and requirements that need to be considered when implementing electronic monitoring of workers. © 2020 ICE Publishing: All rights reserved.

column5: Automated environmental compliance checking requires automated extraction of rules from regulatory textual documents such as energy conservation codes. Before information extraction, text must be classified into predefined categories to filter irrelevant text and group semantically similar text. This paper addresses the problem of developing a domain-specific, machine learning-based hierarchical text classification algorithm that can classify clauses in environmental regulatory documents according to a deep (fifth-level) semantic topic hierarchy, which is more challenging than shallow classification.
column9: Approximately 1,215 clauses collected from 10 environmental/energy efficiency regulatory documents (e.g., IECC 2012, ASHRAE 90.1-2010, LEED), manually labeled with 10 leaf-level energy efficiency subtopics.

column29: Yes - A domain-specific, machine learning-based hierarchical text classification algorithm using SVM with linear kernel, BOW representation, TFIDF weighting, feature selection, and domain-specific stopword removal for classifying environmental regulatory clauses.
column30: The final classifier achieved approximately 97% average recall and 84% average precision on testing data when classifying clauses into 10 leaf-level energy efficiency subtopics. SVM with linear kernel combined with BOW model and TFIDF weighting outperformed other tested configurations, and both feature selection (CHI-based K-best) and domain-specific stopword removal were effective performance improvement strategies. The bigram model underperformed compared to BOW, and modified supervised term weighting schemes did not surpass TFIDF for this application.
column31: Future work includes adapting the TC algorithm to other regulatory documents (e.g., OSHA safety standards), exploring reusability and automated construction of domain-specific stopword lists, investigating other domain adaptation approaches like feature augmentation, and developing an ontology-based TC algorithm to leverage semantic information and compare with the ML-based approach.
column32: Existing construction-domain hierarchical TC work suffers from performance drops at deeper hierarchy levels, handles only binary-transformed multilabel problems with potential data imbalance, lacks domain adaptation (e.g., domain-specific stopwords), and has not tested ensemble ML algorithms or newer supervised term weighting schemes. There is also a lack of benchmark data sets in the construction domain for comparative evaluation.

column40: Automated environmental compliance checking requires automated extraction of rules from environmental regulatory textual documents such as energy conservation codes and EPA regulations. Automated rule extraction requires complex text processing and analysis for information extraction and subsequent formalization of the extracted information into computer-processable rules. In the proposed automated compliance checking (ACC) approach, the text is first classified into predefined categories before information extraction (IE). The advantages are that irrelevant text will be filtered out during text classification (TC) and text with similar semantic meaning will be grouped, thereby improving the efficiency and accuracy of further IE and compliance reasoning (CR). The categories used for TC are predefined in a semantic TC topic hierarchy, and the classified text is subsequently used in semantic IE and semantic CR. This paper presents the proposed machine learning (ML)-based TC algorithm for classifying clauses in environmental regulatory documents based on the TC topic hierarchy. In developing the algorithm, different text preprocessing techniques, ML algorithms, and performance improvement strategies were tested and used. The final TC algorithm was tested on 10 environmental regulatory documents and evaluated in terms of precision and recall. The algorithm achieved approximately 97 and 84% average recall and precision, respectively, on the testing data. © 2015 American Society of Civil Engineers.
